newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Australia's future in Asia, Howard says.
newsitem.headline: Australia's future in Asia, Howard says.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard began a two-stage tour of Asia on Thursday, looking to build relations and put down any suggestions that Australia was a racist society.

"It is a deeply held view of mine that the political and economic destiny of Australia is very much tied up with our successfully being a full-time player in the Asia-Pacific region," he told business leaders in Singapore.

Howard and a business delegation arrived in Singapore late on Wednesday. Howard plans to travel to China on Friday, where he is to meet Chinese Prime Minister Li Peng and President Jiang Zemin. He is due to return to Canberra on April 2.
His trip to China comes after a year of strained ties.
Both sides have acknowledged damaged relations following a series of spats, the latest being China's criticism of Australia's growing military and its foreign policy ties with the United States.
Beijing's ire was also raised by Australian ministerial visits to Taiwan, and Howard's decision to meet exiled Tibetan spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, in 1996.
China is Australia's fifth largest trading partner, with two way trade worth US$6.3 billion in the year to June 30, 1996.

Howard told business leaders that successive Australian governments had essentially a bi-partisan approach to Asia, the thrust of which was "towards an ever increasing commitment to the Asia-Pacific region".
Howard praised the goals of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum and its goal of trade liberalisation.
"Economic prosperity and economic cooperation between nations has in the past been proven to be the foundation of peaceful cooperation," he said.
Australia's relations with some Asian neighbours have also been strained in the past year by worries its was anti-Asian.

In an apparent reference to the recent race debate in Australia and the anti-Asia views expressed by independent Australian MP Pauline Hanson, Howard stressed that Australia was a very open and tolerant society.
"We are immensely proud of the contribution which Australians of Asian descent, whether Chinese or Indian or from any other part of Asia...are making to the future of our country."
Singapore newspapers have carried a series of reports in recent months on racial hostility to Asia and to Singaporeans in particular.
But Howard said the two countries had much in common.
"The people of Singapore...are very welcome in Australia," he said.
Howard told reporters earlier on Thursday that both he and Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong had agreed that China should join the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"One of the messages that I will be repeating to the Chinese government is that we want China to be a full, constructive, positive player in the region. We don't in any way see China in a negative light," Howard told reporters.

"There will be differences. There will always be significant differences betweeen China and Australia on certain issues because we are different societies. But our approach is to focus on the pragmatic, practical, future interest that we have in common."
